description: LORYX is an interactive platform designed to make NASA SPHEREx data easier to explore and understand. SPHEREx observes the sky in 102 infrared spectral bands, producing vast amounts of complex information. LORYX brings these observations together in one accessible space, where users can examine spectra, follow changes over time, and view and compare images of celestial objects. Our mission is to turn astronomical data into clear, explorable evidence and make space science accessible to everyone.
summary:
LORYX is an interactive browser tool that makes real NASA SPHEREx infrared data accessible to students and curious explorers. Users can examine the same sky field across wavelengths and observation dates, explore the 102-channel DR1 spectral cube, compare infrared images with Pan-STARRS1 optical imagery, and create false-color images or time-lapse GIFs. 
Five bundled demonstration fields provide an offline starting point, while online archive access extends exploration to user-entered coordinates. 
For the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, LORYX supports visual investigation of motion and spectral differences through wavelength browsing, time playback, and A/B image comparison. Exports can be downloaded with a separate source-record ZIP so users can trace the observations and display choices. Our initial goal is to lower the technical barrier between public space data and hands-on exploration, while clearly distinguishing visual clues from confirmed scientific discoveries.
details:
LORYX turns real SPHEREx observations into an interactive observing desk. It is designed for students, educators, and astronomy enthusiasts who want to explore infrared data without setting up a scientific programming environment. The project brings wavelength, time, optical context, and creative output into one browser interface.

Users begin with five prepared fields: Barnard's Star, RW Aurigae, Epsilon Indi B, R Draconis, and WISE 0855. They can also enter sky coordinates. Wavelength mode provides individual observations and access to the DR1 spectral cube, with a ribbon showing SPHEREx's 102 nominal channels across six detectors. Reference markers identify selected ice absorption bands without claiming molecular detections. A Pan-STARRS1 optical overlay provides context on the infrared image grid where coverage is available.

Time mode organizes dated exposures on an interactive timeline. Users can play observations, select comparable channels, blink between two images, and inspect a background-subtracted B-minus-A difference image. These functions support the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge by helping users investigate how a source appears across wavelengths and dates, and recognize observations worth further study. The application does not claim a Planet X discovery or automatically validate candidate objects.

The creative output tools produce false-color images, current-frame PNGs, and time-lapse GIFs. An optional image-and-record ZIP includes source URLs, observation information, display settings, and relevant warnings. This connects visual exploration to traceable data instead of separating an attractive image from its origin.

The application uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, Canvas 2D, and WebGL for its introductory sky visualization. Its browser-side data engine reads FITS data from NASA's public archive, interprets image coordinates and available quality information, and projects selected data onto a common viewing grid. An optional JavaScript search service supports automatic archive queries; static hosting can use manual observation-list imports. Five bundled demos work offline, while fresh archive data and the optical overlay require internet access.

We considered accessibility, network delays, data quality, and scientific interpretation. False colors are display choices; the DR1 cube combines visits and is not a time series. Saturation, image alignment, different processing releases, and channel differences can affect comparisons. Brightness plots and difference images are exploratory tools requiring further validation. LORYX wants to make public NASA observations easier to explore, question, and share while keeping these limits visible.

LORYX is a starting point for what we hope to build next. We want to expand its analysis tools, improve usability, and, with suitable hosting and infrastructure, develop it into a reliable public platform for exploring SPHEREx data. This project has strengthened our appreciation of the work behind NASA’s missions and the value of making scientific data openly accessible. We would welcome opportunities to learn from NASA scientists and the wider research community, receive feedback, and contribute to future open-science initiatives. Our ambition is to keep developing LORYX beyond this challenge and help more people explore real observations with curiosity and scientific care.

AI assistance: Claude assisted for application development and the original demo workflow. OpenAI Codex assisted for documentation, verification work, demo revision, and we got help for preparing this submission text.

Astronomical images come from real archive data; AI assistance is not presented as observational evidence.
